claims.text: In non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type alloys, grain size predominantly governs the magnetocaloric response and the sharpness and hysteresis of the magnetostructural transition.
Interfacial lattice strain at grain boundaries predominantly governs the magnetocaloric response and transition hysteresis.
High-ratio differential-speed rolling followed by controlled annealing can refine grain size while keeping bulk composition constant.
Grain refinement increases grain-boundary density or grain-boundary interfacial area.
The proposed thermomechanical treatment will increase interfacial lattice strain.
Grain-boundary regions possess strained lattices, disrupted local chemical order, modified atomic coordination, and defect structures distinct from grain interiors.
Increased grain-boundary density and associated strain distribute the magnetostructural transition over a broader temperature range.
Broadening the magnetostructural transition reduces its abruptness and hysteresis.
Modified grain-boundary coordination changes local magnetic interactions and therefore changes the evolution of magnetic order during cooling.
The as-deposited arc-melted or melt-spun FeMnNiGeSi-type baseline has an ordered, single-phase hexagonal structure.
The baseline material has relatively coarse grains.
Coarse grains in the baseline produce a large, sharp, and hysteretic entropy change.
Bulk baseline samples have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio.
Thermomechanically treated samples will exhibit less magnetocaloric hysteresis than the as-deposited baseline.
Thermomechanically treated samples will exhibit a broader and more gradual transition-temperature profile than the baseline.
The treated samples will retain a significant overall magnetic entropy change suitable for refrigeration.
Chemical ordering, non-grain-boundary residual stresses, or secondary phases may dominate over grain-boundary effects and limit the hypothesis.
